text:
SHORTLY before the IMO’s 21st Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships and its 84th Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting, two leading environmental researchers warn those meetings’ expected focus on biofuels will not solve shipping’s carbon emissions problems.

International Council on Clean Transportation marine programme director Bryan Comer explains that decisions on which fuels will qualify under any IMO climate policy are being developed now, along with their corresponding lifecycle assessment guidelines. Any mistake in drafting those guidelines will take decades to fix, he predicts but, as they stand, they do not account for the emissions that correspond to the “indirect land use change” emissions linked to biofuel production, he says.

Elissama Menezes, co-founder and director of Equal Routes, underlines in the podcast the importance of considering the social and economic sustainability aspects of biofuels, and explains why she believes that, if IMO ignores these impacts of biofuels, “we risk a transition that might look green on paper, but creates significant negative impacts on health, pollution and local economies”.

Both speakers explain that biofuel may appear attractive to regulators because of its cost, but they say that, if shipping adopts biofuel, global demand for it will triple by 2035, leading to significant impacts on other food prices and availability, and to environmental damage caused as more land is turned over to its production.

In their podcast, they also raise a range of other concerns; for example, making biofuels from waste products might perversely encourage fraud and the creation of more waste, Menezes says. She is also concerned about biomethane, which poses the same climate risks as its conventional counterpart as a result of methane slip — which is 80 times more potent than CO2.

To produce biofuels in a sustainable way requires “really strong protections”, Comer says, for example to prevent fraud during its production and to protect human rights, water quality and other environmental aspects.

Such models already exist, he says, citing the International Civil Aviation Organization and the FuelEU Maritime regulation. He goes on to say that e-fuels made using green hydrogen are the best zero-carbon fuels, rather than biofuels.

And Menezes reminds listeners that net zero fuels are not the only way to reduce shipping’s emissions. The starting point, she says, should be “the prioritisation of speed reduction and wind propulsion. These are some of the most effective tools we have”.

text:
Marking a milestone in the construction of the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship, a float-out ceremony was held in Italy for Viking Libra. Once delivered in November 2026, the 54,300-gt cruise ship will be capable of sailing with zero emissions when it begins service in the Mediterranean and Northern Europe.

Viking Cruises chairman and chief executive Torstein Hagen said, “From the beginning, our approach to ship design has focused on reducing fuel consumption, and Viking Libra is our most environmentally friendly vessel yet. Investing in hydrogen was a principled choice for Viking, offering a true zero-emissions solution, and we look forward to welcoming the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship to our fleet.”

The float-out ceremony took place at Fincantieri’s Ancona shipyard, marking the ship’s transition into the final stage of construction. With Viking Libra now afloat, the vessel will be moved to the shipyard’s outfitting dock for final construction and interior build-out.

The ceremony was attended by Fincantieri Ancona shipyard director Gilberto Tobaldi, Viking Cruises executive vice president of product Karine Hagen, and senior vice president of ocean passenger operations Enrico Prunotto.

Classified as a ‘small ship’ by Viking, the luxurious, all-veranda Viking Libra has an overall length of 239 m, a beam of 31 m, nine decks and 499 staterooms for 998 guests.

PEM technology

Viking Libra’s propulsion system will be based partially on liquefied hydrogen and proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells. The fuel cell technology was developed by Isotta Fraschini Motori (IFM), a subsidiary of Fincantieri. The ship’s propulsion system can produce 6 MW of power.

In July 2025, IFM inaugurated a new production line at its Bari, Italy, facility, dedicated to developing and testing hydrogen fuel cell systems. Viking Libra represents one of the first marinised applications of IFM’s PEM fuel cell technology. The ship will have hydrogen stored on board, used both for propulsion and electricity generation.

IFM chief executive Andrea Bochicchio said the project “represents not only a technological advancement, but also a concrete step toward a cleaner and more efficient future.”

According to details revealed by Fincantieri at Seatrade Cruise Global 2025, the auxiliary power generation system based on PEM fuel cells powered by hydrogen will allow for zero-emissions operations in port and in the most environmentally sensitive areas. The system includes two removable tanks of liquefied hydrogen (LH2) that feed two PEM fuel cell containers, supported by a battery system designed to manage load fluctuations through peak shaving to reduce power demand during peak load conditions to cut energy costs and enhance system stability. The electrical power of the PEM fuel cells will be 6.3 MW (2 x 3.15 MW), and the battery capacity will be 4.7 MWh.

This operational profile will allow a zero-emissions mode to be used in protected areas, such as the Norwegian Heritage Fjords, and will include 3 hours of navigation at 10 knots and 10 hours in port. The annual reduction in emissions will be approximately 20% compared with a ship using fossil fuels, assuming LH2 refuelling every two days. The adoption of removable LH2 tanks, which can be easily transported by truck, allows for the immediate effectiveness of the system, even in the absence of a consolidated logistics chain for hydrogen provision in the main cruise ports.

Viking Cruises’ subsequent ocean ship, Viking Astrea, which is also under construction and scheduled for delivery in 2027, will also be hydrogen-powered and capable of operating with zero emissions.

title: Ammonia-to-Power vs. Nuclear-Electric Cargo Ships: Two Zero-Carbon Bets for Heavy Industry
description: Compare ammonia-to-power systems and nuclear-electric cargo ships as they compete to decarbonize heavy industry and shipping using 2026 hardware milestones.
text:
Logistics and manufacturing sectors are currently navigating a high-stakes transition toward decarbonizing heavy industry. While batteries dominate light transport, the race for zero-carbon shipping and industrial heat focuses on two distinct, plausible pathways: distributed ammonia-to-power systems and nuclear-electric propulsion for ultra-large container ships. Ammonia and nuclear solutions solve the same engineering challenge of delivering energy-dense, reliable power where stored electricity fails, yet they follow vastly different infrastructure trajectories.

The shift from theoretical modeling to real-world hardware is accelerating as the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy pushes for zero-emissions shipping solutions. Industry leaders are no longer just comparing engine designs; they are evaluating the entire value chain through the lens of well-to-wake emissions accounting. Separating proven milestones from conceptual proposals highlights the health, safety, and lifecycle caveats that will decide which energy vector achieves mainstream adoption by 2030.

A successful transition between these paths requires more than just comparing energy density math. It requires a grasp of how catalytic ammonia cracking compares to small modular reactors in terms of port acceptance, insurance frameworks, and daily operational reliability. As 2026 pilot projects approach, data from these deployments will finally replace polished narratives with measurable performance indicators.

Energy Density Challenges In Heavy Industry And Global Shipping

Industry Summary: Ammonia Cracking and Nuclear Maritime Rules

Ammonia serves as an effective hydrogen carrier, but tradeoff modeling across production pathways shows climate outcomes depend on production choices and nitrogen emissions controls.

Developers are advancing ammonia-to-hydrogen conversion for industrial power to replace tailpipe-focused fuel swaps with clean electricity generation.

Testing at the Pohang ammonia-to-power pilot in 2026 aims to validate real-world reliability, efficiency, and safety before scaling to larger systems.

Strategic research on nuclear-electric propulsion concepts provides a conceptual design feasibility framework rather than a launch-ready build program.

Maritime emissions pricing and well-to-wake accounting are becoming mandatory under international net-zero shipping rules targeting 2030 milestones.

Why Heavy Industry Keeps Running into the Same Wall

Energy Density and Duty Cycles Set the Baseline

Heavy industries and ocean freight share a fundamental constraint: they need energy-dense power delivered reliably for long durations. While batteries excel in short-haul uses, physical and economic realities make them impractical for continuous industrial duties. Major industrial sectors—including steelmaking furnaces, kilns, and transoceanic container vessels—depend on specialized hydrogen freight corridors to maintain 24/7 operations.

Energy density requirements drive molecules like ammonia and systems like compact nuclear reactors back into policy discussions. Energy-dense solutions answer the baseline requirement, yet they carry very different trade-offs in supply chains, safety, regulation, and emissions.

Why Batteries Break Down at an Industrial Scale

Consider the practical stakes: a regional steel plant operating 24/7 cannot afford a multi-week pause for battery recharging. Likewise, a container ship on a fixed schedule cannot swap out batteries mid-ocean without large port-side infrastructure.

Maintaining high-intensity uptime forces engineers and planners to prioritize energy-dense molecules and long-duration power systems over short-cycle storage. Identifying net-zero industrial pathways helps anchor the need for reality-based reporting in hard-to-abate sectors.

The On-the-Ground Lens Behind the Engineering Math

A short, human vignette: an operations manager once described choosing energy systems the way a mechanic chooses tools, because the wrong choice creates daily workarounds that drain both time and money. Professional insights echo this pragmatic mindset, justifying why these two options warrant careful, reality-based reporting.

Decarbonizing Industrial Heat with Catalytic Ammonia Cracking

Leveraging Existing Infrastructure for Industrial Ammonia Fuel

Ammonia is attractive because it can carry hydrogen in a chemically dense, transportable form. Existing global infrastructure for fertilizer production and transport makes ammonia reuse and repurposing a conceptually appealing strategy.

Advancing green fuel strategies that pair ammonia with e-fuels allows for greater flexibility. When green hydrogen is limited by cost or geography, ammonia acts as a vector moving low-carbon hydrogen over vast distances.

Truly ‘clean’ ammonia demands rigorous lifecycle qualification. Most ammonia today is produced from fossil fuels, and the greenhouse-gas impact depends on how the hydrogen feedstock is made and how emissions are managed across the supply chain. Successful adoption depends on low-carbon production routes, as detailed in the decarbonization roadmap for ammonia technology.

International logistics strategies prove critical to the hydrogen economy. Many credible near-term hydrogen plans involve converting hydrogen into ammonia for export, then cracking it back at the destination, which supports maturing green hydrogen supply chains.

Ammonia Catalytic Cracking: Technical Mechanism and Efficiency

The core technical idea is to split, or crack, ammonia (NH3) into hydrogen (H2) and nitrogen (N2), then use the hydrogen in a fuel cell or hydrogen engine to make electricity. Catalytic cracking eliminates direct ammonia combustion, preventing the generation of nitrogen oxides and reactive pollutants. Lab claims must survive rigorous field conditions where contamination, thermal cycling, and maintenance constraints reveal true commercial performance.

Industry leaders utilize a cracking catalyst designed to boost efficiency, a claim that must be validated in long-duration field operation.

Validating Catalytic Cracking Performance: The 2026 Pohang Pilot

Amogy has described a plan centered on partnerships for ammonia-based distributed power built around a 1 megawatt pilot in 2026, with public-facing scale goals reaching tens of megawatts later in the decade. Field testing provides the only reliable path to validate critical performance metrics. The Pohang demonstration specifically targets:

Conversion efficiency across varying thermal cycles

Operational uptime in industrial environments

Safety protocols for high-pressure handling

System integration with hydrogen engines and fuel cells

These data points determine if catalytic cracking can move from a controlled lab setting into a commercial power plant.

A practical scene to anchor the stakes: an industrial plant manager assessing a distributed ammonia-to-power unit will ask not only about efficiency but also about training requirements, spare parts, sensor reliability, and what happens during a fault. Operational performance metrics—rather than headlines—determine whether pilots scale for industrial use.

Early Adoption Sectors for Distributed Ammonia-To-Power

Localized industrial sectors provide ideal operating profiles for early catalytic cracking adoption. These sectors prioritize localized energy security over large-scale grid connections.

Industrial backup power for continuous manufacturing

Portside auxiliary generation for docked vessels

Remote facilities lacking access to low-carbon electricity

Microgrids requiring long-duration resilience

Logical early destinations provide the controlled environments necessary to refine the technology before a broader commercial rollout. Large-scale green ammonia projects on the Texas Gulf Coast also matter because they decide whether fuel supply can become dependable at industrial scales.

Nuclear-Electric Propulsion for Ultra-Large Container Vessels

Assessing Nuclear Propulsion Feasibility for Cargo Vessels

Strategic research is advancing a nuclear-powered electric propulsion study focused on a 16,000 TEU container ship. The announcement describes a feasibility study and an engineering assessment rather than a build program.

Engineering teams evaluate reactor siting, electric propulsion architecture, and redundancy to establish safety cases. This assessment aims to determine if the concept can meet compliance, insurance, and operational standards within modern maritime frameworks. The baseline legal scaffolding sits inside international conventions for nuclear ship safety, referencing a dedicated nuclear merchant ship safety code written for an earlier era of reactor technology.

Why Nuclear Shows Up Here: Energy Density, Range, and Electric Propulsion Architecture

Modern small modular reactors provide continuous, high-power output without the volumetric penalties of chemical storage. Steady electricity generation allows for efficient distribution across electric propulsion systems. This architecture also grants finer control over shipboard power requirements and system redundancy.

Industry planners chase small modular reactor designs aimed at reducing construction complexity through repeatability and easier certification.

A brief human-scale note: ship crews judge technology by daily operations, maintenance routines, and port reception. The operational lens remains crucial when the system involves a reactor, even if the unit never emits CO2 at point of use.

Scaling Maritime SMRs: The Impact of 100 MW Power Units

Power levels define everything from propulsion architecture to safety systems. Current engineering targets describe modular reactor power supplies around 100 megawatts, signaling a design scale comparable to large conventional marine propulsion systems.

Developing power units at the 100 megawatt scale raises critical engineering questions regarding shielding mass and refueling cycles. It also tests the reliability standards required by global shipping liners.

Navigating diverse regional nuclear policies creates a regulatory landscape as challenging as the engineering itself. This tension is visible in broader planning for mini nuclear stations targeting late-decade commissioning.

Lifecycle Emissions and Supply Chain Transparency

Managing Carbon Intensity in Ammonia Fuel Supply Chains

Ammonia serves as a useful energy carrier, but its climate credentials depend on how its hydrogen feedstock is produced. Production routes utilizing fossil-based hydrogen erode any point-of-use carbon benefit. Success requires tight nitrogen emissions controls and carbon capture throughout the supply chain.

Procurement officers often ask for batch-level carbon intensity documentation rather than relying on generic claims. New guidance for sustainable fuels prioritizes verification and lifecycle accounting to validate regional trade analysis.

Nitrogen Emissions and Environmental Risks: NOx, N2O, and Slip

If ammonia is combusted, or if significant ammonia slips from handling systems, it can produce nitrogen oxides and nitrous oxide, which drive air pollution and contribute strongly to greenhouse warming.

Nitrogen oxides and nitrous oxide drive significant air pollution. Unchecked ammonia combustion risks specifically threaten air-quality outcomes without robust control technology. Detailed analysis of emissions across the ammonia fuel value chain underscores why small leakage rates matter at scale. Cracking-and-fuel-cell approaches serve as a cleaner alternative to burning ammonia directly. Operational guidance on toxicity and bunkering is advancing through DNV’s ammonia-as-a-marine-fuel assessment and a marine fuel safety handbook focused on onboard handling risks.

A minimal, relatable note: anyone who has dealt with a strong ammonia smell in an industrial setting knows it is not a fuel you want leaking. Safety and monitoring are not side issues; they are the project.

Logistical Barriers: Nuclear Safety, Port Access, and Insurance

Nuclear propulsion avoids direct CO2 emissions at point of use but introduces a governance and liability chain including port access policies, insurance frameworks, and emergency planning assumptions.

Modernizing the nuclear ship safety code remains a priority for industry leaders. Outdated 1981 rules currently block port acceptance and commercial underwriting, regardless of engineering soundness.

The practical barrier involves more than engineering. A ship that cannot enter major ports or secure standard insurance cannot run a global schedule.

IMO Zero-Emissions Regulations and Technical Milestones

IMO GHG Strategy and Global Regulatory Pressure

Regulatory frameworks across the maritime sector simultaneously drive and constrain progress in the energy transition. For most operators, compliance math now aligns with the shipping industry’s role in the global energy transition.

The International Maritime Organization is moving toward a net-zero framework that blends lifecycle fuel standards with pricing pressure. This forcing mechanism requires operators to adopt well-to-wake accounting rather than focusing solely on tailpipe emissions.

How the Rules Push Ammonia and Nuclear in Different Directions

For ammonia, lifecycle accounting will favor low-carbon production routes and tight emissions controls, increasing the value of genuinely low-carbon ammonia supply chains. For nuclear, regulatory modernization and international harmonization determine whether ships with onboard reactors can call at major ports.

The Compliance Math Operators Actually Run

A practical example: a shipping company will not select a propulsion technology that increases its risk of detention at port unless the compliance math clearly outweighs those obstacles. Shipping explores multiple tracks, including e-fuel deployment milestones for e-methanol and synthetic fuels.

Upcoming Milestones in Zero-Carbon Industrial Energy

Keeping an eye on these milestones will reveal which technology is gaining true market traction:

Pohang Pilot Performance: Tracking reliability and conversion efficiency from the 1 megawatt pilot will indicate if catalytic cracking works in the field, as described in industry coverage of the Pohang ammonia-to-power demonstration.

Scale Demonstrations: Success depends on whether systems reach multi-megawatt reliability, following the pathways in the IEA ammonia technology roadmap.

Ammonia Fuel Rules: New bunkering protocols will determine if handling can scale responsibly, matching baselines in SGMF’s introduction to ammonia as a marine fuel.

Nuclear Code Revision: The prerequisite for deployment is the MSC-110 tasking to revise nuclear ship safety frameworks.

Port Acceptance Signals: Clear statements from regulators regarding nuclear-propelled ship calls will be the final deciding factor for commercial viability.

Milestones Note

Technology and governance are moving in parallel, clustering both stories into current headlines. Pilot projects push engineering risk into the field, while international bodies revise the rules that decide whether those engineered solutions can operate commercially.

Trust also changes when claims become hardware. The pattern is familiar in climate tech, where measurable performance data tend to outperform polished narratives in building credibility.

Zero-Carbon Industrial Outlook: Comparing Feasibility and Timelines

Ammonia-to-power systems utilizing catalytic cracking currently lead the near-term race, primarily due to existing global fertilizer infrastructure and the 2026 Pohang pilot milestones. If these systems prove reliable and clean ammonia feedstocks scale, they offer a versatile solution for both industrial microgrids and auxiliary maritime power. However, their success remains tethered to rigorous nitrogen emissions controls and the transparency of the green hydrogen supply chain.

Nuclear-electric propulsion remains a high-potential contender for the largest transoceanic routes, yet it faces a more complex timetable. Beyond the engineering of small modular reactors, the path to zero-carbon shipping via nuclear power requires a modernized safety code for nuclear merchant ships and broad port acceptance. Ultimately, the choice between these energy vectors will be decided not just by technical efficiency but by the ability of operators to secure insurance and earn the trust of the communities where these reactors will dock.

Common Questions About Ammonia, Nuclear Ships, and The Energy Transition

Is Ammonia Truly a Clean Fuel for Industrial Use?

Ammonia is carbon-free at the point of use, but its climate value depends on the hydrogen feedstock. Truly green outcomes require renewable energy for production and strict controls to prevent nitrogen oxide emissions.

How Does Ammonia Cracking Support Zero-Carbon Shipping?

Cracking splits ammonia into hydrogen and nitrogen, allowing the hydrogen to power fuel cells or engines without combustion. This method avoids the air quality risks associated with burning ammonia directly.

What are the Main Barriers for Nuclear-Electric Cargo Ships?

While technically feasible, these ships face significant hurdles in port acceptance, maritime insurance, and outdated international safety codes. Regulatory harmonization is required before commercial deployment can begin.

Why are Energy Density and Duty Cycles Important for Industry?

Heavy industries like steelmaking and long-haul shipping require massive power for weeks at a time. Batteries currently lack the density to sustain these cycles, making energy-dense molecules or reactors necessary.

What is the Significance of the 2026 Pohang Pilot?

The Pohang pilot is a one-megawatt demonstration of ammonia-to-power technology. It will provide the first real-world data on conversion efficiency and operational safety at an industrial scale.

title: US calls on IMO to cancel October vote on Net-Zero Framework, craft new proposal
description:
The organization in April 2025 took a step toward establishing a legally binding framework to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships globally, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by or near 2050.
The proposed framework is the first of its kind to combine mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing across an entire industry sector.
A vote to formally adopt the framework was expected to be held during the extraordinary session of the MEPC, which convened Oct. 14-17, 2025.
“The IMO Net-Zero Framework would also stretch the Organization far beyond its mission, turning it into a global climate bank.
Furthermore, planned recipients of the IMO-controlled fund could expect to receive pennies on the dollar compared to the economic hardship that the IMO Net-Zero Framework would create in their broader economic landscape.
text:
The U.S. government is continuing to advocate against the adoption of the United Nations International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net Zero Framework, stating it “would have dire economic consequences for the shipping industry, energy producers, and global consumers.”

The IMO is a specialized agency of the UN that regulates maritime transport. The organization in April 2025 took a step toward establishing a legally binding framework to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships globally, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by or near 2050. The proposed framework is the first of its kind to combine mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing across an entire industry sector.

The Net Zero Framework was approved by the IMO’s Marine Environmental Protection Committee in April. A vote to formally adopt the framework was expected to be held during the extraordinary session of the MEPC, which convened Oct. 14-17, 2025. The IMO, however, on Oct. 17 announced efforts to formally adopt the framework will be delayed for one year, with the extraordinary session set to reconvene in October 2026.

The MEPC is scheduled to hold its 84th session from April 27 through May 1. The meeting is expected to focus on mid-term GHG reduction measures.

In preparation for that meeting, the U.S. on March 6 submitted comments to the MEPC regarding the committee’s proposals. “Specifically, any framework must avoid economic penalties or levies, carbon taxes, or multilateral funds that would burden the shipping industry and its consumers,” the U.S. said in a summary of its comments. “Regulations must not disadvantage any fuel types, including conventional fuels, LNG, nuclear, biomass-based fuels, or other marine propulsion technologies, and should welcome an ‘energy-all’ approach. Any framework must ensure reliability for existing fleets and avoid disruption to global trade, with emissions reduction targets based on current market conditions rather than arbitrary end-state goals.”

Within the comments, the U.S. states that the net-zero framework approved in April 2025 “would have dire economic consequences for the shipping industry, energy producers, and global consumers.

“The framework would unwisely promote the use of expensive, unproven, and unavailable fuels in lieu of existing and proven technologies that fuel global shipping fleets,” the U.S. continued. “The IMO Net-Zero Framework would also stretch the Organization far beyond its mission, turning it into a global climate bank. Furthermore, planned recipients of the IMO-controlled fund could expect to receive pennies on the dollar compared to the economic hardship that the IMO Net-Zero Framework would create in their broader economic landscape. These significant shortcomings risk the reliability and stability of the international shipping industry, along with the global supply chains and economic activity which so heavily depend on shipping.”

The comments also emphasize that the U.S. “remains strongly apposed to the IMO Net-Zero Framework” and calls for the IMO to “end consideration” of the framework and cancel the vote scheduled to take place in October 2026.

The U.S. also suggests that any new proposal offered by the IMO exclude any economic elements, such as a financial penalty, carbon tax or levy. According to the U.S., any new proposal should also be crafted to exclude penalties or limits on fuel types, including those related to conventional crude or diesel, LNG, nuclear, biomass-based fuels, or any other type of marine propulsion technology. To ensure reliability for the shipping industry’s existing fleet, the U.S. also indicates any new proposal should eliminate penalties on LNG, recognize biofuels as viable marine fuels, and support industry-led advances in alternative fuels without picking winners or losers via regulations.

text:
A broad coalition of maritime industry organizations has formally called on Member States of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to adopt its Net-Zero Framework in 2026, describing it as a decisive step toward eliminating greenhouse gas emissions from shipping by or around 2050. Calls have emerged urging the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to formally recognise wind propulsion as a cornerstone of its Net-Zero Framework (NZF). The calls come ahead of the MEPC 2nd Extraordinary Session in London this week.

USA obstructs en threatens

Previously, during the second extraordinary session of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC/ES.2), held in October 2025, the United States strongly opposed the proposed Net-Zero Framework. U.S. officials framed the plan as an economically harmful global carbon tax and actively lobbied other countries to reject or delay it. According to a joint statement released by Secretary of State Rubio, Secretary of Energy Wright, and Secretary of Transportation, the Administration unequivocally rejects this proposal before the IMO and will not tolerate any action that increases costs for our citizens, energy providers, shipping companies and their customers, or tourists.

As stated, the economic impacts from this measure could be disastrous, with some estimates forecasting global shipping costs increasing as much as 10% or more. Furthermore, the NZF proposal poses significant risks to the global economy and subjects not just Americans, but all IMO member states to an unsanctioned global tax regime that levies punitive and regressive financial penalties, which could be avoided. The United States is considering the following actions against nations that support this global carbon tax on American consumers:

Pursuing investigations and considering potential regulations to combat anti-competitive practices from certain flagged countries and potential blocking vessels registered in those countries from U.S. ports;

Imposing visa restrictions including an increase in fees and processing, mandatory re-interview requirements and/or revisions of quotas for C-1/D maritime crew member visas;

Imposing commercial penalties stemming from U.S. government contracts including new commercial ships, liquified natural gas terminals and infrastructure, and/or other financial penalties on ships flagged under nations in favor of the NZF;

Imposing additional port fees on ships owned, operated, or flagged by countries supporting the framework; and

Evaluating sanctions on officials sponsoring activist-driven climate policies that would burden American consumers, among other measures under consideration.

Pivotal moment

Shipping stands at a pivotal juncture. The upcoming decisions could determine whether the sector accelerates toward meaningful decarbonisation or stalls in delay and uncertainty. Technology providers, sustainability advocates, and industry coalitions are united in the belief that consistent recognition of wind energy, as championed by the International Windship Association (IWSA), is essential to achieving a practical and equitable pathway to net-zero emissions.

Positioning wind alongside alternative fuels

The IWSA’s submission to MEPC/ES.2 emphasises: ‘Wind is free at source and the only truly zero-emission energy available at scale to the global fleet today.’ By systematically integrating wind within the NZF, the IMO can deliver a framework that is neutral, transparent, and fair, positioning wind alongside alternative fuels and energy efficiency solutions. The NZF has the potential to act as a global signal providing certainty to unlock finance, accelerate innovation, and scale proven technologies. But that power depends on consistent accounting across the sector. Without it, distortions in technology uptake, compliance, and funding allocation could slow the pace of progress, state the parties behind the call. As the IWSA notes, consistent treatment of wind is a litmus test for the IMO’s commitment to technology and energy-source neutrality. The organisation also stresses that wind propulsion should be integrated from the outset, not treated as a late-stage addition.

A practical path forward

As discussions intensify, industry consensus is emerging around several key principles:

Neutrality, not exceptions – Wind must be recognised as a zero-carbon energy source, with full inclusion in intensity and compliance frameworks.

Data and verification – The IWSA proposes streamlined methods to capture and validate wind energy contributions through the IMO Data Collection System.

Fair access to funding – Wind propulsion should be proportionately rewarded within the NZF Fund, supporting early fleet-scale adoption.

Scalability and co-benefits – Wind delivers fuel savings, operational resilience, and immediate emissions reductions—available for both newbuilds and retrofits.

Maintain a global lane – A unified NZF is far more effective than fragmented national regimes, ensuring competitiveness and clarity for all actors.

Also read: Wind-assisted ship propulsion nears tipping point for rapid adoption

Industry alignment

Organisations across the maritime sector are working to deliver technologies that reduce emissions now, technologies that maintain vessel performance and commercial viability. Wind-assist solutions, already proven and deployable at scale, offer a reliable and complementary path alongside emerging fuels.

“Rapid adoption of the IMO’s Net‑Zero Framework in 2026 would send a powerful signal to producers and investors that Europe is committed to a global, level‑playing‑field transition, unlocking the clean fuel volumes shipping urgently needs.”

Maarten Wetselaar, CEO, Moeve.

text:
Korean Register (KR) has released a research report analyzing the safety challenges associated with hydrogen-fueled ships and outlining key risk factors and mitigation measures to support the safe adoption of hydrogen in the maritime sector.

The publication comes amid growing international efforts to establish regulatory frameworks for hydrogen as a marine fuel. At the 11th session of the International Maritime Organization’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (IMO CCC), draft interim guidelines for the safety of ships using hydrogen as fuel were developed. The guidelines are expected to receive final approval at the 111th session of the Maritime Safety Committee (MSC), scheduled for May 2026.

Hydrogen, which emits no carbon during combustion, is gaining attention as a promising alternative fuel for maritime decarbonization. It can also serve as a feedstock for producing other alternative fuels such as methanol, suggesting that hydrogen-based fuel supply chains are likely to expand in the future. As international trade and transportation of hydrogen increase, demand for hydrogen carriers and hydrogen-fueled ships is also expected to grow.

However, hydrogen presents several safety challenges due to its unique physical and chemical properties. These include high flammability and explosion risks, hydrogen embrittlement, and the need for extreme storage conditions compared with conventional marine fuels.

For safe onboard storage and use, hydrogen must be handled either as compressed hydrogen or liquefied hydrogen. This requires storage under extremely high pressures—hundreds of times atmospheric pressure—or at cryogenic temperatures of approximately −253°C. As a result, ensuring the safety and reliability of hydrogen fuel containment systems, fuel supply systems, and related onboard infrastructure has become a key technical priority.

To support the commercialization of hydrogen as a marine fuel and enhance industry understanding of its safety implications, KR developed the report as a technical reference for the maritime sector. The publication provides an overview of maritime hydrogen systems, analyzes hydrogen-related accident cases, identifies key hazards and mitigation strategies, and reviews relevant international regulations.

KIM Daeheon, Executive Vice President of KR, stated, “We hope this research will serve as a useful reference for industry, academia, and research institutions involved in the development of hydrogen-fueled ships. We will continue to support our customers and the maritime industry by advancing technology development and sharing the latest technical knowledge to help address evolving environmental regulations.”

text:
China has called on the IMO to accelerate work on onboard carbon capture (OCCS), warning that regulatory delays could undermine growing industry interest in the technology.

The country pushed back against efforts to exclude OCCS pathways from default lifecycle emission values, saying such an approach is “inappropriate,” it said in a proposal submission to the IMO on March 17.

It warned that removing OCCS from the framework risks distorting comparisons between competing decarbonisation solutions.

The document added that the view that “pathways including OCCS were not suitable for a default emission value at this stage” could give other emerging technologies an unintended advantage.

China also urged caution in defining lifecycle boundaries for OCCS, noting operational uncertainties and limited shipping experience.

“It would be challenging for shipowners to assume responsibility for the fate of the CO2 after offload,” it said.

The submission further highlighted gaps in current technical work, stating that “no work plan, timeline, or interim calculation formula has been provided,” which could “stall the review cycle” for key emission factors.

While several IMO workstreams are examining OCCS issues such as monitoring and verification, China warned progress “may not fully keep pace with the significant investment interest currently being demonstrated by the market”.

It urged the IMO to avoid premature conclusions and ensure regulatory frameworks leave room for OCCS to develop as a viable emissions-reduction pathway.

Carbon capture technology enables CO2 emissions from a ship’s exhaust to be captured and stored onboard for discharge ashore.

The system can be installed on the existing fleet, helping reduce emissions.
